Addiction is a chronic, relapsing brain disease characterized by the compulsive use of a substance or engagement in a behavior despite harmful consequences. It involves a loss of control, intense cravings, and a shift in brain reward circuits that prioritizes the habit over normal activities. 

-Key Aspects of the Best Definitions:

-Brain Disease: Addiction alters brain tissue and function, particularly in the reward, motivation, and memory systems.
Compulsive Behavior: The inability to stop using a substance or engaging in a behavior despite knowing it causes harm.
-Physical/Psychological Dependence: Often involves withdrawal symptoms and a need for the substance to function normally.
-Wide Scope: Covers substance use (drugs, alcohol, nicotine) and behaviors (gambling, shopping).


-Medical/Clinical: Defined by the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) as a chronic disease of brain reward, motivation, memory, and related circuitry.
-Functional: The Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction (CAMH) describes it as a compulsive need, often involving harmful consequences to one's health and life.
-Expert Insight: Dr. Gabor Maté often defines addiction as an attempt to escape deep emotional pain, focusing on the root causes rather than just the behavior. 

If you or someone you know is struggling, resources are available through the SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-HELP) in the US, or the NHS addiction services in the UK.

Eternal Return is one of the few games with an unusual genre, combining both battle royale and MOBA-style PvP. It is safe to say that the game is one of a kind. Some of its unique mechanics include a loot & craft system, zone restrictions instead of the typical shrinking circle found in most normal battle royale games.

Eternal Return can feel intimidating at first, especially for new players, because there are just too many things to learn, from characters to crafting to routing and because the game itself is very fast-paced. However, once you start to understand how the game works, it becomes extremely rewarding, as you plan out your character builds, optimize your route across the map, and coordinate plays with your team. Mastering these is part of the game but, once you're able to do it, each match turns into a satisfying mix of tactical decision-making and precise plays, making the game both challenging and fun.

Eternal Return has a lot of appeal, with its biggest positives being the satisfying dopamine rush you get from winning matches and executing well-planned strategies, as well as the high-quality character designs and artwork. On the downside, the game has a steep learning curve, which can be discouraging for new players. Depending on the server, long queue times and language barriers can also make the experience less smooth, and progressing through the battle pass requires a significant amount of grinding.

Like many beginners, I initially gave up on Eternal Return because of its difficulty. But later, I came back and actually tried to understand the game. Now, I have over 700 hours of playtime, and I’ve learned that no match ever goes exactly as planned. Each game is different, and the key is adapting to the situation and the flow of the match. With a good team that comms well, winning at least once every five matches isn’t too difficult. That said, the battle pass still remains as a huge pain in the ass to grind for, unless you just play a lot.

Overall, Eternal Return is a unique and challenging game that rewards patience, strategy, and teamwork. Its combination of battle royale and MOBA mechanics, along with features like crafting, route planning, and team play, makes every match feel fresh and exciting. While the learning curve can be steep and the battle pass grind is real, the satisfaction of mastering the game and pulling off a play now and then more than makes up for it.

Personally, I’d give it a solid 8.5/10. Although the game is difficult to get into at first, once you understand it, everything starts to make sense. Matches tend to follow a similar flow but differ more in the mid to late game, and mastering character mechanics like a one-shot combo can make a difference. The process can be challenging, but it’s absolutely worth the time. If you’re looking for something new or different and don't mind a challenge, I highly suggest giving Eternal Return a try. Who knows… you might get hooked even harder than I did.

Eternal Return, developed by Nimble Neuron and published by Nimble Neuron with distribution support from SapStaR Games in some regions, is a multiplayer strategy game that merges several genres into one distinctive competitive experience. At first glance it resembles a battle royale, but it quickly becomes clear that the game also draws heavily from multiplayer online battle arenas and survival crafting systems. Matches unfold from a top-down perspective on the mysterious Lumia Island, where players must gather resources, craft equipment, and eliminate rival contestants until only one team or survivor remains. By combining character-based combat with strategic planning and resource management, Eternal Return creates a gameplay loop that is both fast-paced and intellectually demanding.

The game’s setting provides an intriguing backdrop for its competitive structure. Lumia Island is the site of secret experiments conducted by a powerful organization known as AGLAIA. Participants are placed on the island as test subjects and forced to fight each other under controlled conditions. Each experiment ends with the survivors emerging victorious, only for the process to begin again after memories are reset. This narrative framework explains the cyclical nature of the gameplay while introducing a cast of characters with distinct personalities, motivations, and backgrounds. Although the story largely unfolds through character lore and optional content rather than direct narrative sequences, it adds flavor to the world and helps differentiate the characters beyond their gameplay abilities.

The core gameplay revolves around survival and preparation before direct combat begins. At the start of each match, players choose a character and enter the island with minimal equipment. Instead of searching for randomly generated weapons like in most battle royale games, players must gather specific materials and craft the items they need. Every weapon, armor piece, and accessory requires particular components that can be found in different regions of the map. Because of this system, planning an efficient route across the island becomes one of the most important skills in the game. Experienced players often memorize crafting routes that allow them to quickly collect the necessary materials for powerful equipment before encountering opponents.

This crafting system significantly alters the pace and strategy of matches. Early stages often focus on exploration and resource gathering, with players avoiding unnecessary fights while building their preferred loadout. As time progresses and more zones of the island become restricted, surviving players are forced closer together. The later stages then transform into intense tactical battles where character abilities, positioning, and teamwork determine the outcome. The transition from quiet preparation to chaotic combat creates a satisfying rhythm that keeps matches engaging from beginning to end.

Combat itself is heavily influenced by MOBA design. Each character possesses a set of unique abilities that can be upgraded during the match, allowing players to tailor their approach depending on the situation. Some characters specialize in quick melee attacks and mobility, while others rely on ranged weapons, traps, or supportive abilities that benefit teammates. Because fights occur from a top-down perspective, awareness of positioning and skill timing becomes extremely important. Landing a well-timed ability or coordinating attacks with teammates can instantly turn the tide of battle.

The island’s design further deepens the strategic elements of gameplay. Lumia Island is divided into numerous zones, each containing specific materials and wildlife that can be hunted for additional resources. Over time, certain areas become restricted due to experimental conditions imposed by AGLAIA, forcing players to relocate and eventually converge toward central locations. This system encourages constant movement across the map and prevents players from remaining hidden in one place for too long. Learning which zones contain particular crafting materials and how they connect geographically is essential for mastering the game.

Another defining feature of Eternal Return is its large and varied roster of characters. Each character comes with unique weapons, abilities, and recommended crafting builds that influence how they perform in combat. Some characters excel at aggressive close-range fighting, while others specialize in long-distance attacks, traps, or defensive tactics. This diversity allows players to experiment with different playstyles and strategies. Mastery of a character often requires not only learning their abilities but also understanding which equipment combinations best complement their strengths.

Visually, the game adopts a vibrant anime-inspired aesthetic paired with a clean 2.5D top-down perspective. Characters are designed with colorful outfits and distinctive personalities that make them easy to recognize during matches. The environments of Lumia Island vary widely, including urban districts, forests, research facilities, and industrial zones. Despite the variety of locations, the visual clarity remains strong, allowing players to quickly identify enemies, abilities, and environmental objects during fast-paced combat.

The developers have also implemented systems that encourage long-term engagement. Players can unlock additional characters, cosmetic items, and seasonal content as they continue playing. Ranked modes provide a competitive ladder for players seeking to measure their skills against others, while regular updates introduce balance adjustments and new characters to keep the gameplay evolving. This ongoing support has helped maintain an active player base and a growing competitive scene.

Despite its many strengths, Eternal Return can be intimidating for newcomers. The game’s combination of crafting mechanics, map knowledge, and character abilities creates a steep learning curve. New players may initially struggle to understand optimal crafting routes or effective combat strategies, especially when facing experienced opponents who have already mastered these systems. Matches can also feel unforgiving, as mistakes during early stages may leave players under-equipped when encounters with stronger enemies occur.

Even so, the complexity is also what gives the game its long-term appeal. Once players begin to understand the crafting system, character abilities, and map dynamics, each match becomes an engaging strategic challenge. The sense of satisfaction that comes from executing a well-planned route, building powerful equipment, and outmaneuvering opponents in the final stages is one of the game’s greatest rewards.

Eternal Return ultimately stands out within the crowded multiplayer landscape because of how successfully it blends different genres into a cohesive experience. By combining battle royale survival, MOBA-style combat, and intricate crafting mechanics, the game creates a competitive environment where knowledge, preparation, and teamwork matter just as much as mechanical skill. For players willing to invest time into learning its systems, Eternal Return offers a deep and highly strategic multiplayer experience that continues to evolve with each update.

Is Eternal Return Worth Making Your "Main" Game?

I’m going to be very honest and recommend this review to anyone considering making this their main MOBA.

First of all, this game can be simply described as a Battle Royale MOBA. You play in teams of 3 (current standard) and build your character using resources you scavenge around the map. Each district has its own specific item pool. After finishing your "early build," you have to contest exclusive resources (like Meteorites, Tree of Life or map bosses) to craft your legendary "late-game build." If you prefer a safer route, you earn Credits to buy the items you’d otherwise have to fight for—though it takes longer.

The game is fair, but it is heavily reliant on strategy, character mastery, and situational analysis. In my opinion, this is the hardest MOBA to introduce someone to. The mechanics are simple, but the depth of knowledge required is massive, which scares off a lot of new players. Mastering a character here is harder than in League of Legends, for example. Most characters (with exceptions like Fiora) have mechanics that look simple on paper but must be used completely differently in high-level practice. Every character requires a steep learning curve, which is exactly why I personally love Eternal Return.

I started playing in 2020, one month after release. I didn't play frequently over the years, but recently I’ve been playing daily to blow off some steam.

Here are my main considerations if you want to make this your main game:

CONS:
- Small Player Base (Especially SA): The South American player base is small. Ranked matches can be impossible to find outside of the season start, and mid-tier rankings often feel dead. Normal Games can sometimes be harder than Ranked because the matchmaking varies so wildly.

- Ego & Toxicity: Because the game is difficult, "ego players" are a real problem, even though not frequently. Some players suffer from the Dunning-Kruger effect—they make bad calls, refuse to admit they are wrong, and ruin the match. It’s more frustrating than anything I’ve experienced in League.

- Lack of Coordination: Some players treat this strictly as a solo game. They wander off alone, ignore objectives, and die. This is very frequent in Normal Games.

- Team Synergy is Critical: Drafting matters. If someone picks a character that doesn't fit the team composition, you feel it immediately. Some characters simply won't function well without the right setup. (can be a PRO for some)

- High Commitment: You really have to dedicate yourself to your main characters to see results. (can be a PRO for some)

PROS:
- Unique Dynamic: It is a seamless blend of MOBA combat and Battle Royale tension. Fighting for objectives creates unique game dynamics that feel unmatched by other titles.

- Rewarding Difficulty: The characters are hard to learn, but satisfying to master. I struggled with my current mains, even dropping them a few times, but once it "clicked," I fell in love. Pro tip: Watch YouTube guides; they are essential for understanding specific combos.

- Tactical Depth: It’s not just "how to play your character," but "when to play" and "how to adapt to your teammates." This adds a layer of excitement to drafting that goes beyond just getting kills.

- Strategic Kills: Kills give you rewards and loot, but they aren't the only thing that matters. You can win through smart play and macro, not just by being a K/D/A chaser.

- The Victory Lap: The feeling of hitting #1 after a good match is unmatched.

Verdict: I strongly recommend Eternal Return if you are looking for a challenge and want a game with a higher skill ceiling. It requires effort to learn, but speaking for myself, it was absolutely worth it.

Hours Played: 3
Get dragged into a haunting world where fluid combat and survival lore collide into post-apocalypse. Imaginative tool-building in its doomsday setting transforms items to create challenges that feel fluid.

I couldn't get the sound to work during matches, and for some reason when I tried multiple attempts to install again it provided no fixes. As a player who heavily leans toward sound design as atmosphere there was little depth with no audio enhancements then had thought maybe that is how most people play the battle arena style games with sound off. It is something I overlooked then ultimately the reason I stopped.

Coming back after a while, they've made a lot of changes that make the game much more approachable. No more needing to manage mana, food gets automatically consumed, more gadgets and events around the map to help you not fall behind.

The characters and their kits and the biggest highlight.
There's basic and regular characters with guns and swords that do what would expect. Then there's themes like figure skater, firefighter, musician, racer that get explored well. Then there's the delightfully unique like a baseball player that plays like Draven, a combo mage that summons chess pieces, and MMA fighter that creates a ring to fight in. With the variety of kits there's sure to be a character that works for everyone, and even the more "basic" characters that punch, kick, and shoot still feel unique from one another.

There's also a lot of familiarity if you're familiar with other MOBAs, especially League. Magus ult / Sion ult, Irem's and Nidalee's forms, Isol's mines and Teemo's shrooms, William's and Draven's auto attack minigame, the list goes on.

Which leads into my biggest gripe with the game: Sound Design.
At least in English, a lot of the characters sound bored out of their minds and extremely flat. For a battle royal, survive the experiment by killing others, I would have expected much more energy from the characters. Some abilities also lack that defining punch.

Take Magnus' ult and Sion's ult. Magnus rides his motorcycle into you vroom vroom style. Cool and stylish, but it's only the hum of the engine you hear. Sion yells loud enough for everyone to hear as he charges.

Debi & Marlene's ult and Yone's ult. The difference is subtle, but Yone's ult feels like it packs much more of a punch, both visually and audibly.

Shioichi and Katarina when they pick up knives. There's a weight to Katarina as she spins to collect a knife and more of a visual effect as she teleports to each one. Shiochi just... appears at a knife, and if you're playing him you get a "ding" to indicate that you did indeed teleport to a knife. Cool, but could be so much better.

Combat and larger team fights can get very visually busy, and can feel extremely fast.
Especially for newer players it lands closer to League than HotS for the amount of visual clutter (aka, more visual clutter). Many characters create circles/zones of abilities or have some type of counter or parry that can get lost in the sauce during a fight. Against certain characters you could get blown up by them and not understand what happened, but I feel many games with MOBA characters have that same issue.

Alright so things have improved. It seems like a lot of mechanics and systems got streamlined to be less convoluted.. Thank god! There's no more mana! Builds come online much much faster, and you don't need to go to 6 different areas to reach your base purple items. Character kits also seem to have been adjusted and streamlined. TL;DR: its somewhat fun, but you basically lose interest after 15-20 matches.
- 'bad-tier' DPS characters literally cannot compete with other DPS characters even under optimal conditions for their kit, despite being designed as DPS and having little to no support/tank attributes. There are basically some characters you should just never choose ever, even if you like their aesthetic. 

- The flow of the the match is poorly designed. Early game you basically do almost zero damage to anyone, so everyone just walks around and collects materials and basically ignores enemy teams. Late game, basically every team can reach full late-game items even when behind. At that point, the ONLY way to get better gear is to contest some of the rare spawns (Dr. Wickerline, Rifts), and even then some of the items you can build out of the rare drops are only marginally better, and only one person in your team will get to choose one marginally better item per event. There is only a small window in the MID GAME where a player that has been playing well has an equipment/level advantage over others.
It basically just comes down to which team has the most cracked characters, and how well they can stick together and click buttons on the correct enemy targets.

As someone who’s played League of Legends for a decade, I wasn’t expecting another MOBA-style game to grab my interest. But Eternal Return managed to do it by mixing in fresh ideas and cutting down on the overwhelming complexity that drives a lot of new players away from the genre.

Overall, I’m enjoying this game more than I thought I would. I played League of Legends for 10 years, so this game wasn’t all that hard to understand. They make it pretty easy for players since there are premade builds for each character. The hardest part, like in any other MOBA, is learning what each character does.

Thankfully, unlike League, this game doesn’t have 171 characters you need to memorize just to play properly. That’s one of the main reasons I never got into games like DOTA 2 or Smite. it always felt like a massive time investment just to learn all the character abilities while also figuring out your lane, farming, jungle rotations, and so on.

So discovering Eternal Return, a game with MOBA-style combat, a nicely sized roster, and some fresh mechanics I haven’t seen in more traditional MOBAs, has been a breath of fresh air.

However, a few things are holding the game back. For one, the queue times are long, be ready to wait 5–10 minutes for a match. And if someone goes AFK, everyone gets sent back to queue for another 5–10 minutes. I think this will improve as more people discover the game.

Second, I swear that about a quarter of the time I use my abilities, they don’t register. Sometimes I have to spam the same ability just to get it to go off. This might be by design, I think your cursor can’t exceed the distance of your skill shots, which prevents them from registering. If that’s true, it’s super annoying.

It's a battle royale of 8 teams of 3 in the form of a MOBA . You move with right clic , use spells with QWER .

This game is pretty generous in term of gifts and rewards, you can get a lot of free cosmetics (  skins , emotes , backgrounds , etc...),

What I like most about this game is the gameplay loop , you can feel your progress in every part of the game :
-Optimising your loadout to allow you to have the best preparation possible (you can always select recommended ones). 
-How fast you complete your items early game .
-Where and how to farm animals optimally .
-Your decision making when it comes to moving on the map , what objective to contest.
-Your skill level , some characters are extremely demanding in terms of clics and awareness .

As you can see from what I previously stated , I totally recommend this game . 
Biggest issue imo is the lack of players in some regions that can make queue time pretty long depending on when you are trying to play , but don't give up , I hope you will be able to see why I love this game .

Used to remember there was Solo/Duo mode. Now it's gone? 

Generally, the game's quite... unique so to speak. The unique mix of crafting, survival, and anime-style BR combat was genuinely refreshing. But the recent direction this game has taken is killing everything that made it fun for solo and duo players. Now we’re forced to match into trios, and unless you're in a pre-made squad on Discord, you’re cannon fodder. The matchmaking is brutal and totally unfair.

New characters often release overtuned, older ones are forgotten, and the meta shifts feel artificial—like you're being forced to pick what's “popular” instead of what fits your playstyle.

Eternal Return had a soul when it welcomed all player types—solo, duo, casuals, and hardcore. Now, unless you’re running a sweaty 3-stack, this game punishes you just for showing up. Compare that to something like Naraka: Bladepoint—it has beautiful combat, solo-friendly options, fairer matchmaking, and more frequent balancing. Even older games like Battlerite Royale (RIP) had better fundamentals than what ER is offering right now.

Unless the devs bring back solo/duo matchmaking and listen to actual community feedback, this game will bleed players until only the hardcore trio squads remain.
